Anatomy.question: ১) Umbilical cord contains-
Anatomy.exp:
The umbilical cord normally contains:

  • Two umbilical arteries

  • One umbilical vein

  • Wharton's jelly, a gelatinous connective tissue that protects the umbilical vessels from compression.

High-Yield

  • Umbilical cord = 2 arteries + 1 vein + Wharton's jelly

  • Umbilical vein: Carries oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus.

  • Umbilical arteries: Carry deoxygenated blood from fetus to placenta.

Rapid Recall

  • AVA mnemonic: Arteries = 2, Vein = 1

  • Wharton's jelly → Protects umbilical vessels

  • Single umbilical artery → May be associated with congenital anomalies

Anatomy.question: ২) Layer of epidermis only present in thick skin
৩) Predominant cell type of epidermis
Anatomy.exp:
Keratinocytes are the predominant cell type of the epidermis, accounting for approximately 90–95% of all epidermal cells. They produce keratin, which provides the skin with its protective barrier.

High-Yield

Cell Function
Keratinocyte Produces keratin; forms 90–95% of epidermal cells
Melanocyte Produces melanin
Langerhans cell Antigen-presenting immune cell
Merkel cell Touch receptor

Rapid Recall

  • Keratinocyte → Keratin → Most abundant

  • Melanocyte → Melanin

  • Langerhans → APC (immune)

  • Merkel → Touch sensation

Anatomy.question: ৪) The most abundant type of cerebral cortical neurons are the
Anatomy.exp:
Pyramidal cells are the most abundant neurons of the cerebral cortex, constituting approximately 70–80% of cortical neurons. They are excitatory (glutamatergic) projection neurons and are found predominantly in layers III and V of the cerebral cortex.

Rapid Recall

  • Cerebral cortex → Pyramidal cell

  • Cerebellum → Purkinje cell

  • Pyramidal cells → Glutamate (excitatory)

  • Purkinje cells → GABA (inhibitory)

Anatomy.question: ৫) Most numerous papillae of tongue
Anatomy.exp:
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the dorsum of the tongue. They are keratinized, provide a mechanical function (grip and friction), and do not contain taste buds.

Rapid Recall

  • Most numerous → Filiform

  • No taste buds → Filiform

  • Largest → Circumvallate

  • Mushroom-shaped → Fungiform

  • Lateral border → Foliate

Anatomy.question: ৬) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Anatomy.exp:
The hippocampus is the principal structure responsible for memory consolidation, i.e., converting recent (short-term) memory into long-term memory. Bilateral hippocampal damage results in anterograde amnesia, where new long-term memories cannot be formed.

Rapid Recall

  • Hippocampus → Memory consolidation

  • Amygdala → Fear & emotion

  • Bilateral hippocampal lesion → Anterograde amnesia

  • Basal ganglia (Putamen + Globus pallidus) → Movement

Anatomy.question: ৭) Which hormone stimulates Osteoclast activity?
৮) Capillaries only have
Anatomy.exp:
Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels and their wall consists of a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane. They do not have tunica media or tunica adventitia.

Although capillaries are composed of the tunica intima, the defining structural component is endothelium. In anatomy/histology MCQs, the expected answer is endothelium.

Rapid Recall

  • Capillaries → Single layer of endothelium

  • Exchange vessels → Capillaries

  • Smallest blood vessels

  • No media or adventitia

Anatomy.question: ৯) Which hormone suppresses immune cell activities?
১০) Most predominant cell type in pancreatic islets
১১) The following structures are derived from endoderm :
Anatomy.exp:
Reference-langman’s medical embryology/13th/P-86

The parathyroid glands develop from the endoderm of the pharyngeal pouches:

  • Superior parathyroids → 4th pharyngeal pouch

  • Inferior parathyroids → 3rd pharyngeal pouch

Rapid Recall

  • Endoderm → "Gut and Glands"

    • Parathyroid

    • Thyroid follicular cells

    • Thymus epithelium

  • Mesoderm → Spleen

  • Ectoderm → Pituitary, Inner ear

Anatomy.question: ১২) Subdivision of prosencephalon
১৩) Cortical area number assigned for taste sensation
১৪) Medial lobe of cerebrum is mainly supplied by
Anatomy.exp:
The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes of the cerebrum, including the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory areas for the lower limb).

The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) supplies the medial temporal and occipital lobes, while the middle cerebral artery (MCA) supplies most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemispheres.

Anatomy.question: ১৫) Nucleus of hypothalamus involved in oxytocin synthesis
১৬) L5 cord segment correspond which thoracic vertebrae?
Anatomy.exp:
Because the spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral column, the lumbar spinal cord segments lie opposite lower thoracic vertebrae.

The L5 spinal cord segment is located approximately opposite the T12 vertebra.

Anatomy.question: ১৭) By the beginning of 4th month, maternal and fetal circulation is separated by the-
Anatomy.exp:
By the beginning of the 4th month, the cytotrophoblast has largely disappeared from most chorionic villi, making the placental membrane thinner to facilitate maternal–fetal exchange.

The principal barrier separating the maternal and fetal circulations is the syncytiotrophoblast (syncytium), together with the fetal capillary endothelium and a thin connective tissue layer. Among the given options, the best single answer is syncytium.

High-Yield

  • Early placental membrane:

    1. Syncytiotrophoblast

    2. Cytotrophoblast

    3. Villous connective tissue

    4. Fetal capillary endothelium

  • After the 4th month:

    • Cytotrophoblast largely disappears

    • Placental membrane becomes thinner

    • Exchange becomes more efficient

Rapid Recall

  • 4th month → Cytotrophoblast disappears

  • Main trophoblastic barrier → Syncytiotrophoblast

  • Maternal and fetal blood normally do not mix

Anatomy.question: ১৮) Innermost muscular layer of stomach
Anatomy.exp:
The muscularis externa of the stomach is unique because it has three layers of smooth muscle:

  1. Inner oblique ✔

  2. Middle circular

  3. Outer longitudinal

The inner oblique layer helps the stomach perform powerful churning and mixing movements.

Anatomy.question: ১৯) Inlet of inguinal canal situated in-
Anatomy.exp:
The inlet (deep inguinal ring) of the inguinal canal is an opening in the transversalis fascia, located approximately 1.25 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

Rapid Recall

  • Deep ring (Inlet) → Transversalis fascia

  • Superficial ring (Outlet) → External oblique aponeurosis

  • Deep ring is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels

  • Indirect inguinal hernia enters through the deep inguinal ring

Anatomy.question: ২০) Main artery of stomach
Anatomy.exp:
The left gastric artery is considered the main artery of the stomach. It is the smallest branch of the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature and adjacent anterior and posterior walls of the stomach. It also gives esophageal branches.

High-Yield

Arterial supply of the stomach:

  • Left gastric artery → Lesser curvature (main artery)

  • Right gastric artery → Lesser curvature

  • Left gastroepiploic artery → Greater curvature

  • Right gastroepiploic artery → Greater curvature

  • Short gastric arteries → Fundus

Rapid Recall

  • Main artery of stomach → Left gastric artery

  • Origin → Celiac trunk

  • Fundus → Short gastric arteries (from splenic artery)

  • Greater curvature → Gastroepiploic arteries

Anatomy.question: ২১) Most dilated part of GIT—
Anatomy.exp:
The stomach is the most dilated part of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT). It serves as a temporary reservoir for food and performs mechanical and chemical digestion before emptying into the duodenum.

High-Yield

  • Most dilated part of GIT → Stomach

  • Most fixed part of small intestine → Duodenum

  • Longest part of GIT → Small intestine

  • Largest gland → Liver

Rapid Recall

  • Most dilated GIT → Stomach

  • Food reservoir → Stomach

  • Rectum → Stores feces

  • Anus → Terminal opening of GIT

Anatomy.question: ২২) Most common position of appendix -
Anatomy.exp:
The retrocecal position is the most common position of the vermiform appendix, occurring in approximately 60–65% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies behind the cecum.

High-Yield

Positions of the appendix (approximate frequency):

  1. Retrocecal – 60–65% (most common)

  2. Pelvic – 25–30%

  3. Subcecal

  4. Preileal

  5. Postileal

Rapid Recall

  • Most common position → Retrocecal

  • Most common artery → Appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic artery)

  • McBurney's point → Surface marking of the base of the appendix

  • Pain of acute appendicitis: Periumbilical → Right iliac fossa

Anatomy.question: ২৩) Principal artery of Rectum—
Anatomy.exp:
The superior rectal artery is the principal arterial supply of the rectum. It is the terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) and supplies the upper two-thirds of the rectum.

Rapid Recall

  • Principal artery of rectum → Superior rectal artery

  • Superior rectal = Continuation of IMA

  • Middle rectal = Internal iliac

  • Inferior rectal = Internal pudendal

Anatomy.question: ২৪) Most dependent part of abdomen in lying position -
Anatomy.exp:
In a supine (lying) position, the hepatorenal pouch (Morrison's pouch) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity. It is the first site where fluid such as blood, pus, or ascitic fluid accumulates in a patient lying on their back.

High-Yield

  • Supine position → Hepatorenal pouch (Morrison's pouch)

  • Standing position → Rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas) in females; Rectovesical pouch in males

  • FAST ultrasound examines Morrison's pouch for free intraperitoneal fluid.

Rapid Recall

  • Supine → Morrison's pouch

  • Standing female → Pouch of Douglas

  • Standing male → Rectovesical pouch

  • First site of intraperitoneal fluid accumulation in trauma → Morrison's pouch

Anatomy.question: ২৫) True ligament of liver—
Anatomy.exp:
A true ligament of the liver is a fibrous remnant of a fetal structure and is not formed by peritoneum. Ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the ductus venosus, making it a true ligament.

High-Yield

True ligaments of the liver:

  • Ligamentum teres hepatis → Remnant of the left umbilical vein

  • Ligamentum venosum → Remnant of the ductus venosus

False (peritoneal) ligaments:

  • Falciform ligament

  • Coronary ligament

  • Right and left triangular ligaments

  • Lesser omentum

Rapid Recall

  • Ligamentum venosum → Ductus venosus (true ligament)

  • Ligamentum teres → Left umbilical vein (true ligament)

  • Falciform & Coronary → Peritoneal (false) ligaments

Anatomy.question: ২৬) Main support of liver -
Anatomy.exp:
The main support of the liver is provided by the surrounding abdominal viscera together with intra-abdominal pressure. The peritoneal ligaments help maintain its position but are not the primary support.

High-Yield

  • Main support of liver → Surrounding viscera + intra-abdominal pressure

  • Secondary supports → Falciform, coronary, triangular ligaments and lesser omentum

  • Bare area of the liver is attached directly to the diaphragm.

Rapid Recall

  • Primary support → Surrounding viscera

  • Ligaments → Secondary support

  • Bare area → Direct contact with diaphragm

  • Largest gland → Liver

Anatomy.question: ২৭) Organ with purely serous covering
২৮) Serous demilune are present in
২৯) Results of fertilization-
Anatomy.option2: Completion of first meiotic divison of the ovum
Anatomy.option3: Determination of the sex of the embryo
Anatomy.exp:
Fertilization results in the formation of a zygote, restoration of the diploid chromosome number, initiation of cleavage, and determination of the genetic sex of the embryo. The sex is determined at fertilization by whether the fertilizing sperm carries an X or Y chromosome.

High-Yield

Results of fertilization:

  • Formation of a zygote

  • Restoration of the diploid chromosome number (46)

  • Determination of genetic sex (XX/XY)

  • Completion of the second meiotic division of the oocyte

  • Initiation of cleavage

Rapid Recall

  • Fertilization → Completes meiosis II

  • Sex determined at fertilization

  • Zona reaction prevents polyspermy

  • Cleavage starts after fertilization

Anatomy.question: ৩০) The most common type of cardiac septal defect is :
Anatomy.option1: Muscular type ventricular septal defect or VSD
Anatomy.option2: Secudum type atrial septal defect or ASD
Anatomy.exp:
The most common congenital cardiac septal defect is a ventricular septal defect (VSD), and the membranous (perimembranous) type accounts for about 70–80% of all VSDs.

High-Yield

  • Most common congenital cardiac defect → VSD

  • Most common VSD → Membranous (perimembranous) VSD

  • Most common ASD → Ostium secundum ASD

Rapid Recall

  • Overall septal defect → Membranous VSD

  • Most common ASD → Ostium secundum

  • Membranous septum develops from endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges

  • Small VSDs may close spontaneously

Anatomy.question: ৩১) Thickest layer of adrenal gland
৩২) Chromaffin cells are present in
Anatomy.exp:
Chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons located in the adrenal medulla. They secrete catecholamines—primarily adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine)—in response to sympathetic stimulation.

High-Yield

  • Chromaffin cells = Modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons

  • Location → Adrenal medulla

  • Secretion → Adrenaline (~80%) and Noradrenaline (~20%)

  • Embryological origin → Neural crest cells

Rapid Recall

  • Chromaffin cells → Adrenal medulla

  • Origin → Neural crest

  • Hormones → Adrenaline & Noradrenaline

  • Stimulated by → Preganglionic sympathetic fibers (ACh)

Anatomy.question: ৩৩) Butterfly shaped gland
Anatomy.exp:
The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped endocrine gland located in the anterior neck. It consists of two lateral lobes connected by a central isthmus, giving it its characteristic butterfly appearance.

High-Yield

  • Butterfly-shaped gland → Thyroid

  • Largest endocrine gland → Thyroid

  • Follicular cells → T₃ & T₄

  • Parafollicular (C) cells → Calcitonin

Rapid Recall

  • Butterfly-shaped → Thyroid

  • Two lobes + isthmus

  • Largest endocrine gland

  • Embryological origin → Endoderm (C cells from neural crest via the ultimobranchial body)

Anatomy.question: ৩৪) What causes venous blood to return to the heart?
Anatomy.option1: The pumping action of the heart.
Anatomy.option2: The squashing action of muscles, and valves in the veins.
Anatomy.option3: Rhythmic vasoconstriction and valves in the veins.
Anatomy.option4: Gravity, valves and the negative pressure generated by the atria emptying.
Anatomy.exp:
Venous return from the limbs depends mainly on the skeletal muscle pump. Contraction of skeletal muscles compresses the veins, propelling blood toward the heart, while venous valves prevent backflow and ensure one-way flow.

High-Yield

Factors promoting venous return:

  • Skeletal muscle pump (most important in the limbs)

  • Venous valves

  • Respiratory pump (negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration)

  • Sympathetic venoconstriction

  • Cardiac suction (minor contribution)

Rapid Recall

  • Main mechanism → Skeletal muscle pump + venous valves

  • Inspiration → Increases venous return

  • Venous valves → Prevent backflow

  • Gravity ↓ Venous return from lower limbs when standing

Anatomy.question: ৩৫) Which one is site of phonation?
৩৬) Which cardiac vein drains directly into Right atrium?
Anatomy.exp:
The anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior wall of the right ventricle and empty directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus.

High-Yield

Cardiac venous drainage:

Vein Drains into
Great cardiac vein Coronary sinus
Middle cardiac vein Coronary sinus
Small cardiac vein Coronary sinus
Anterior cardiac veins Right atrium (directly)
Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins) Directly into all heart chambers (mainly right atrium and right ventricle)

Rapid Recall

  • Directly into right atrium → Anterior cardiac veins

  • Main venous drainage of heart → Coronary sinus

  • Coronary sinus opens into → Right atrium

  • Thebesian veins → Drain directly into cardiac chambers

Anatomy.question: ৩৭) Which forms an electrical “barrier” between the atria and ventricles so that they contract independently?
Anatomy.exp:
The fibrous skeleton of the heart is a dense connective tissue framework that electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. This prevents direct spread of electrical impulses from the atrial myocardium to the ventricular myocardium. The only normal electrical connection between the atria and ventricles is through the atrioventricular (AV) node and the His bundle.

High-Yield

  • Fibrous skeleton → Electrical insulation between atria & ventricles

  • Only normal conduction pathway → AV node → Bundle of His

  • SA node → Normal pacemaker (60–100/min)

  • AV node → Physiological delay (~0.1 second)

Rapid Recall

  • Electrical barrier → Fibrous skeleton

  • Only bridge → AV node & Bundle of His

  • SA node → Pacemaker

  • Papillary muscles → Prevent valve prolapse

Anatomy.question: ৩৮) Which is the embryologic counterpart to the right middle lobe of lung?
Anatomy.exp:
The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe and is the embryological (and anatomical) counterpart of the right middle lobe. Because the heart occupies space on the left side (forming the cardiac notch), the left lung has two lobes instead of three.

High-Yield

  • Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower)

  • Left lung: 2 lobes (upper, lower) + lingula

  • Lingula is part of the left upper lobe and corresponds to the right middle lobe.

Rapid Recall

  • Embryological counterpart of right middle lobe → Lingula

  • Left lung → 2 lobes + lingula

  • Cardiac notch → Left lung

  • Right lung → 3 lobes

Anatomy.question: ৩৯) The vertebral level where trachea begins
Anatomy.exp:
The trachea begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, opposite the C6 vertebra, as a continuation of the larynx. It descends into the thorax and bifurcates at the carina opposite the sternal angle (T4–T5 level).

High-Yield

  • Trachea begins → C6 (lower border of cricoid cartilage)

  • Trachea ends (carina) → T4–T5 (sternal angle)

  • Length of trachea → ~10–12 cm

  • Cartilaginous rings → 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings

Rapid Recall

  • Start → C6

  • Bifurcation (carina) → T4–T5

  • Cricoid cartilage → C6

  • Sternal angle → T4–T5 (carina)

Anatomy.question: ৪০) Closure of the foramen primum results from fusion of the :
Anatomy.option1: Septum secondum and the fused endocardial cushions
Anatomy.option2: Septum secondum and the septum primum
Anatomy.option3: Septum primum and the fused endocardial cushions
Anatomy.option4: Septum primum and the septum spurium
Anatomy.exp:
During atrial septation, the septum primum grows downward from the roof of the primitive atrium toward the fused endocardial cushions. The gap between them is the foramen primum. As the septum primum fuses with the fused endocardial cushions, the foramen primum closes. Before complete closure, apoptosis in the upper part of the septum primum creates the foramen secundum, maintaining right-to-left atrial shunting in fetal life.

High-Yield

  • Foramen primum → Closes by fusion of septum primum with endocardial cushions.

  • Foramen secundum → Forms by apoptosis in the upper part of the septum primum.

  • Septum secundum → Forms the foramen ovale.

  • Failure of endocardial cushion fusion → Ostium primum ASD (AV septal defect).

Rapid Recall

  • Foramen primum closes → Septum primum + endocardial cushions

  • Foramen secundum forms → Apoptosis in septum primum

  • Foramen ovale → Septum secundum

  • Endocardial cushions → AV septum and AV valves

Anatomy.question: ৪১) Ostium secondum defect :
Anatomy.option1: Is characterized by a large opening between left and right atria
Anatomy.option2: May be caused by excessive resorption of septum primum
Anatomy.option3: May be accompanied by intracardiac shunting of blood
Anatomy.option4: All of the above are correct
Anatomy.exp:
An ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is the most common type of ASD. It usually results from excessive resorption of the septum primum or inadequate development of the septum secundum, leaving a persistent opening in the interatrial septum. This defect permits left-to-right intracardiac shunting after birth.

High-Yield

  • Most common ASD → Ostium secundum ASD

  • Cause → Excessive resorption of septum primum or deficient septum secundum

  • Shunt → Left-to-right

  • Complication → Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial/right ventricular enlargement, atrial arrhythmias

Rapid Recall

  • Most common ASD → Ostium secundum

  • Embryological defect → Septum primum resorption

  • Left-to-right shunt

  • Fixed wide splitting of S₂ → Classic clinical sign

Anatomy.question: ৪২) Of the following the most closely associated with the portal vein is:
Anatomy.exp:
The portal vein develops from the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) veins, which drain blood from the yolk sac to the primitive heart. During embryogenesis, anastomoses between the right and left vitelline veins give rise to the portal venous system.

Rapid Recall

  • Portal vein → Vitelline veins

  • Ligamentum teres → Umbilical vein

  • Ligamentum venosum → Ductus venosus

  • Common carotid artery → 3rd aortic arch

Anatomy.question: ৪৩) The foramen cecum of the adult tongue:
Anatomy.option1: Make the point of embryonic evagination of the thymus gland
Anatomy.option2: Make the point of embryonic evagination of the thyroid gland
Anatomy.option3: Divides the tongue into two parts, an anterior one-third and a posterior two-third
Anatomy.exp:
The foramen cecum is a small pit located at the apex of the sulcus terminalis on the dorsum of the tongue. It represents the site of origin (evagination) of the thyroid diverticulum, from which the thyroid gland develops and descends through the thyroglossal duct.

High-Yield

  • Foramen cecum → Origin of thyroid diverticulum

  • Thyroglossal duct extends from the foramen cecum to the developing thyroid

  • Persistence of the thyroglossal duct → Thyroglossal duct cyst

  • Sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3

Rapid Recall

  • Foramen cecum → Thyroid origin

  • Thyroglossal duct begins at foramen cecum

  • Sulcus terminalis → 2/3 anterior + 1/3 posterior tongue

  • Thymus → 3rd pharyngeal pouch

Anatomy.question: ৪৪) In the third week of human embryonic development :
Anatomy.option2: A bilaminar embryonic disc is formed
Anatomy.option3: The body stalk moves ventrally and joins with the yolk sac stalk to form the umbilical cord
Anatomy.option4: The neural plate is induced by the notochordal process and associated mesoderm
Anatomy.exp:
The third week of embryonic development is known as the week of gastrulation. During this week, the notochordal process forms and induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, marking the beginning of neurulation.

High-Yield

Third week events:

  • Gastrulation → Formation of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm

  • Primitive streak appears

  • Notochord develops

  • Neural plate is induced (beginning of neurulation)

  • First blood vessels and heart primordium begin to form

Rapid Recall

  • 2nd week → Bilaminar disc, amnion, yolk sac

  • 3rd week → Gastrulation, primitive streak, notochord, neural plate

  • 4th week → Neural tube closure, embryonic folding, umbilical cord formation

Anatomy.question: ৪৫) Capacitation of the sperm :
Anatomy.option1: Is caused by the zona pellucida
Anatomy.option4: Removes the head of the sperm
Anatomy.exp:
Capacitation is the functional maturation of sperm that occurs in the female reproductive tract. It removes glycoproteins and seminal plasma proteins from the sperm membrane, enabling the sperm to undergo the acrosome reaction, penetrate the zona pellucida, and fertilize the oocyte. Therefore, capacitation is essential for fertilization.

High-Yield

  • Capacitation

    • Occurs in the female genital tract

    • Takes about 7 hours

    • Enables the acrosome reaction

    • Essential for fertilization

  • Acrosome reaction

    • Triggered by zona pellucida (ZP3)

    • Releases enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase) to penetrate the zona pellucida

Rapid Recall

  • Capacitation → Female reproductive tract

  • ZP3 → Triggers acrosome reaction

  • Cortical (zona) reaction → Prevents polyspermy

  • Capacitation is essential for fertilization

Anatomy.question: ৪৬) The cloaca is divided into the anorectal canal & the primitive urogenital sinus by the :
Anatomy.exp:
The cloaca is the terminal end of the embryonic hindgut. During the 4th–7th weeks, the urorectal septum grows caudally and divides the cloaca into:

  • Anterior → Primitive urogenital sinus

  • Posterior → Anorectal canal

When the urorectal septum reaches the cloacal membrane, it divides it into the urogenital membrane and the anal membrane.

High-Yield

  • Cloaca → Divided by urorectal septum

  • Anterior part → Primitive urogenital sinus

  • Posterior part → Anorectal canal

  • Cloacal membrane → Divided into urogenital membrane + anal membrane

  • Failure of urorectal septum development → Anorectal malformations (e.g., imperforate anus, rectourethral fistula)

Rapid Recall

  • Divider of cloaca → Urorectal septum

  • Anterior → Urogenital sinus

  • Posterior → Anorectal canal

  • Weeks → 4th–7th embryonic weeks

Anatomy.question: ৪৭) Payers patches are predominantly found in
৪৮) Most numerous main glands of prostate are contained within
৪৯) Uterine artery is a branch of which artery?
Anatomy.exp:
The uterine artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It courses medially within the base of the broad ligament and crosses superior to the ureter ("Water under the bridge": Ureter = water, Uterine artery = bridge).

High-Yield

  • Origin: Anterior division of the internal iliac artery

  • Crosses: Above the ureter ("Water under the bridge")

  • Supplies: Uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and uterine tube (via tubal branches)

  • Anastomoses: Ovarian artery

Rapid Recall

  • Uterine artery → Internal iliac artery

  • Uterine artery crosses over ureter

  • Mnemonic → "Water under the bridge"

  • Anastomosis → Ovarian artery

Anatomy.question: ৫০) Somatostatin is secreted from which cell?
৫১) Urethra passes through which part of penis?
৫২) Which cranial nerve supplies lateral rectus muscle?
৫৩) Normal cell in CSF
৫৪) Dermatome of umbilicus
৫৫) Which cell is a respiratory macrophage?
Anatomy.exp:
Dust cells are the alveolar macrophages of the lungs. They reside within the alveoli and phagocytose dust particles, microorganisms, and cellular debris, helping to keep the alveoli clean and contributing to pulmonary defense.

Rapid Recall

  • Dust cell → Lung (alveolar macrophage)

  • Kupffer cell → Liver

  • Microglia → CNS

  • Langerhans cell → Skin

  • Histiocyte → General tissue macrophage

Anatomy.question: ৫৬) The lymphatic organs responsible for filtration of blood-
Anatomy.exp:
The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ and is responsible for filtering blood. It removes aged or damaged red blood cells, blood-borne microorganisms, and initiates immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

Rapid Recall

  • Spleen → Filters blood

  • Lymph node → Filters lymph

  • Thymus → T-cell maturation

  • Tonsils → Guard the entrance of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts

Anatomy.question: ৫৭) Which one is the primary lymphatic organ?
Anatomy.exp:
Primary (central) lymphoid organs are where lymphocytes develop and mature. In humans, these are:

  • Bone marrow → B-cell maturation

  • Thymus → T-cell maturation

Among the given options, only the thymus is a primary lymphoid organ.

Rapid Recall

  • Primary lymphoid organs → Bone marrow, Thymus

  • Thymus → T-cell maturation

  • Bone marrow → B-cell maturation

  • Spleen → Filters blood

  • Lymph node → Filters lymph

Anatomy.question: ৫৮) Regarding cell distribution of intermediate filaments, which one is not true?
Anatomy.exp:
Nestin is an intermediate filament protein expressed primarily in neural stem cells and neuroepithelial progenitor cells, not in mature neurons. Mature neurons characteristically express neurofilaments (NF-L, NF-M, NF-H).

Rapid Recall

  • Keratin → Epithelium

  • Desmin → Muscle

  • Vimentin → Mesenchyme

  • GFAP → Astrocytes

  • Neurofilament → Mature neurons

  • Nestin → Neural stem cells

  • Lamins → Nucleus of nucleated cells

Anatomy.question: ৫৯) The sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and migrate towards the opposite pole during-
Anatomy.exp:
During anaphase of mitosis, the centromeres divide, allowing the sister chromatids of each chromosome to separate and migrate to opposite poles of the cell via the spindle fibers.

High-Yield Mitosis Sequence

  • Prophase → Chromosomes condense; spindle forms.

  • Metaphase → Chromosomes align at the equator.

  • Anaphase → Sister chromatids separate and migrate to opposite poles.

  • Telophase → Nuclear membranes reform; chromosomes decondense.

  • Cytokinesis → Cytoplasm divides, producing two daughter cells.

Rapid Recall

  • PMAT

    • P = Prophase → Prepare

    • M = Metaphase → Middle

    • A = Anaphase → Apart

    • T = Telophase → Two nuclei

Anatomy.question: ৬০) Regarding G2 phase which one is correct?
Anatomy.option1: Cells synthesize RNA and protein essential to DNA replication
Anatomy.exp:
The G₂ phase is the period after DNA replication (S phase) and before mitosis (M phase). During G₂, the cell:

  • Synthesizes proteins needed for mitosis.

  • Accumulates ATP (energy) for mitosis.

  • Checks and repairs replicated DNA (G₂ checkpoint).

Rapid Recall

  • G₁ → Growth

  • S → DNA Synthesis

  • G₂ → Get Ready for Mitosis

  • M → Mitosis

Anatomy.question: ৬১) Which organelle sorts and packages proteins within a cell?
Anatomy.exp:
The Golgi apparatus is the cell's sorting, modifying, packaging, and shipping center. Proteins synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) are transported to the Golgi, where they undergo further modification (e.g., glycosylation), are sorted, and packaged into vesicles for secretion, lysosomes, or the plasma membrane.

Rapid Recall

  • RER → Makes proteins

  • Golgi → Modifies, packages, and ships proteins

  • SER → Makes lipids

  • Lysosome → Digests

  • Mitochondria → Makes ATP

Anatomy.question: ৬২) The organelles playing an important role in intracellular digestion of the phagocytosed particles are-
Anatomy.exp:
Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing acid hydrolases that digest phagocytosed particles, microorganisms, and worn-out cellular components. After phagocytosis, the phagosome fuses with the lysosome to form a phagolysosome, where intracellular digestion occurs.

Rapid Recall

  • Lysosome → Digestion

  • Phagosome + Lysosome = Phagolysosome

  • Peroxisome → H₂O₂ detoxification (catalase)

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

  • Mitochondria → ATP production

Anatomy.question: ৬৩) Unipolar neuron
৬৪) Basal nuclei exclude
Anatomy.exp:
The basal nuclei (basal ganglia) are collections of gray matter located deep within the cerebral hemispheres. They include the corpus striatum (caudate nucleus + lentiform nucleus), claustrum, and amygdaloid body (classically included in anatomical descriptions, though functionally part of the limbic system).

The emboliform nucleus is not a basal nucleus. It is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei.

High-Yield

Basal nuclei (classical anatomy)

  • Corpus striatum

    • Caudate nucleus

    • Lentiform nucleus (Putamen + Globus pallidus)

  • Claustrum

  • Amygdaloid body

Deep cerebellar nuclei (Lateral → Medial)

  • Dentate

  • Emboliform

  • Globose

  • Fastigial

Rapid Recall

  • Basal nuclei → Corpus striatum, Claustrum, Amygdala (classical)

  • Emboliform → Deep cerebellar nucleus

  • Mnemonic (Deep cerebellar nuclei): Don't Eat Greasy Food

    • Dentate

    • Emboliform

    • Globose

    • Fastigial

Anatomy.question: ৬৫) Neuroglial cell located in peripheral ganglia
৬৬) Which junction helps in the heart’s co-ordinated beats?
Anatomy.exp:
Gap junctions (nexus) are specialized intercellular junctions that allow the direct passage of ions and small signaling molecules (e.g., Ca²⁺, cAMP, cGMP) between adjacent cells. In cardiac muscle, they provide electrical coupling, enabling rapid spread of action potentials and ensuring coordinated contraction (synchronized heartbeat).

Rapid Recall

  • Gap junction (Nexus) → Heart's coordinated beats

  • Desmosome → Mechanical strength

  • Tight junction → Barrier/seal

  • Zonula adherens → Cell adhesion

  • Hemidesmosome → Cell to basement membrane

Anatomy.question: ৬৭) Which one is the major constituent of plasma membrane?
Anatomy.exp:
The correct answer is protein. Proteins are the major constituent of the plasma membrane by mass and are responsible for most membrane functions.

Components of plasma membrane:

Protein (~50% by mass) → Transport, receptors, enzymes, cell signalling

Phospholipid (~40%) → Forms the lipid bilayer framework

Cholesterol → Maintains membrane fluidity and stability

Carbohydrate → Cell recognition and glycocalyx formation

The other options are incorrect because:

Phospholipid → Major structural component but not the major constituent by mass.

Cholesterol → Regulates fluidity, but present in smaller amounts.

Carbohydrate → Minor component attached to proteins/lipids.

High-yield cell biology recall:
Major constituent of plasma membrane (by mass) = Protein
Basic structural framework = Phospholipid bilayer

Exam pearl:
Plasma membrane = Lipid bilayer + proteins; proteins are the major functional component.

Anatomy.question: ৬৮) Primary ossification centre are in
Anatomy.exp:
The primary ossification center develops in the diaphysis (shaft) of a long bone during fetal life. It is the first site where cartilage is replaced by bone in endochondral ossification.

The secondary ossification centers appear later, usually after birth, in the epiphyses.

Rapid Recall

  • Primary ossification → Diaphysis

  • Secondary ossification → Epiphysis

  • Epiphyseal plate → Longitudinal bone growth

  • Metaphysis → Most active growth region; common site of osteomyelitis in children

Anatomy.question: ৬৯) Which one propels sperm?
৭০) Which Cytoplasmic organelle is membrane bound?
৭১) Osteocytes are found in
Anatomy.exp:
Osteocytes are mature bone cells derived from osteoblasts. They are located in lacunae, small cavities within the mineralized bone matrix. Their cytoplasmic processes extend through canaliculi to communicate with adjacent osteocytes.

Rapid Recall

  • Osteoblast → Builds bone

  • Osteocyte → Lives in lacunae

  • Osteoclast → Resorbs bone

  • Canaliculi → Communication between osteocytes

  • Lamellae → Concentric bone layers

Anatomy.question: ৭২) Most abundant constituent of bone matrix
Anatomy.exp:
The bone matrix consists of an organic component (mainly type I collagen) and an inorganic component. The most abundant inorganic constituent is calcium hydroxyapatite crystals Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2Ca10​(PO4​)6​(OH)2​, which provide hardness and compressive strength to bone.

High-Yield Bone Matrix Composition

Component Percentage Function
Type I collagen ~90% of organic matrix Tensile strength
Calcium hydroxyapatite Major inorganic component Hardness & compressive strength

Rapid Recall

  • Major organic matrix → Type I collagen

  • Major inorganic matrix → Calcium hydroxyapatite

  • Osteoblast → Bone formation

  • Osteoclast → Bone resorption

  • Osteocyte → Maintenance of bone matrix

৭৪) Tissue with very small amount of extracellular matrix
৭৫) Example of stratified columnar epithelium
৭৬) Simple coiled tubular gland is present in

৭৮) Which cell produces antibody?
৭৯) Most common cell in connective tissue proper
Anatomy.exp:
Fibroblasts are the most numerous (most common) cells in connective tissue proper. They are responsible for the synthesis and maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM), including collagen fibers, elastic fibers, reticular fibers, and ground substance.

High-Yield Connective Tissue Cells

Cell Primary Function
Fibroblast Produces collagen, elastic fibers, and ground substance
Macrophage Phagocytosis and antigen presentation
Plasma cell Antibody production
Mast cell Histamine and heparin release
Adipocyte Fat storage

Rapid Recall

  • Most common CT cell → Fibroblast

  • Most common CT fiber → Type I collagen

  • Plasma cell → Antibody production

  • Macrophage → Phagocytosis

  • Mast cell → Histamine, allergic reactions

৯০) Central tendon of diaphragm develops from
Anatomy.exp:
The central tendon of the diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, a thick plate of mesoderm that initially lies between the thoracic cavity and the yolk sac. It forms the central tendinous portion of the diaphragm.

  • Septum transversum → Central tendon

  • Pleuroperitoneal membranes → Posterolateral diaphragm

৯২) Nerve for 3rd pharyngeal arch
৯৩) Derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch

৯৬) Brown fat-
Anatomy.option1: Richer in mitochondria than ordinary fat
Anatomy.option2: Nucleus is situated at the periphery
Anatomy.exp:
Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is specialized for non-shivering thermogenesis. It contains numerous mitochondria rich in cytochromes, giving it its characteristic brown color. These mitochondria express uncoupling protein-1 (UCP-1/thermogenin), which generates heat instead of ATP.

Rapid Recall

  • Brown fat → Multilocular

  • Brown fat → Numerous mitochondria (UCP-1)

  • Brown fat → Central nucleus

  • Brown fat → Highly vascular

  • Brown fat → Non-shivering thermogenesis

Anatomy.question: ৯৭) Regarding histology of thyroid gland-
Anatomy.option1: Follicular cells are squamous when stimulated
Anatomy.option2: Parafollicular cells are smaller than follicular cells
Anatomy.option3: Each follicle consists of a simple epithelium and a central lumen
Anatomy.exp:
The thyroid gland is composed of numerous spherical follicles. Each follicle is lined by a single layer (simple epithelium) of follicular cells surrounding a central lumen filled with colloid (thyroglobulin).

Rapid Recall

  • Active follicular cells → Columnar

  • Inactive follicular cells → Squamous/flattened

  • C cells → Calcitonin

  • Chief cells (parathyroid) → PTH

  • Thyroid follicle = Simple epithelium + Colloid-filled central lumen

Anatomy.question: ৯৮) Regarding skeletal muscle-
Anatomy.option3: Nucleus is single, oval and central
Anatomy.exp:
Skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleated, and show prominent cross-striations due to the regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments.

Rapid Recall

  • Skeletal → Striated, voluntary

  • Long, cylindrical, unbranched

  • Multinucleated with peripheral nuclei

  • No gap junctions

Anatomy.question: ৯৯) Regarding goblet cells-
Anatomy.option3: Nucleus is present towards the apex
Anatomy.exp:
Goblet cells are unicellular exocrine glands found in the respiratory and intestinal epithelium. They synthesize and secrete mucin, which becomes mucus after hydration.

Rapid Recall

  • Goblet cell → Mucus

  • Exocrine, not endocrine

  • Broad apical portion

  • Basal flattened nucleus

  • Found in respiratory and intestinal epithelium

Anatomy.question: ১০০) Myoepithelial cells are not present in -
Anatomy.exp:
Myoepithelial cells are contractile cells located between the epithelial cells and the basement membrane of exocrine glands. They help expel glandular secretions into ducts. The thyroid gland is an endocrine gland and therefore does not contain myoepithelial cells.

Rapid Recall

  • Myoepithelial cells = "Basket cells"

  • Found only in exocrine glands

  • Function → Contract to expel secretions

  • Absent in endocrine glands (e.g., thyroid)
